title: On Cybernetics and Transcendental Philosophy
speaker: Gotthard Günther
note: English translation of the original German lecture. Light editorial smoothing for readability; technical terms preserved.
paragraphs: When we consider organisms, they possess the capacity to form an image of their environment — meaning, it belongs to the essence of matter that in its objective existence it possesses the capacity for self-reflection. It is easy to see that the idealist opposition of immanence and transcendence must lead, first, to a radically two-valued logic and, second, in the course of the history of science, to a rigorous separation between the natural sciences and the humanities.

The same affinity exists between two-valued logic and materialism. In order to explain the cosmos out of itself, the materialist must make a metaphysical assumption: he must assert — and deeper materialist thinkers like Lenin or Ernst Bloch have done so — that matter is not detached, but stands in a relation to itself. That is to say: it is self-reflecting and self-imaging objective being.

The duality of the materialist world manifests itself here in the opposition between the being of matter and the image of its own existence. For formal logic — which has only a deaf ear for ideological prejudices and incantations — the abyss between immanence and transcendence is just as deep as that between material being and the images that being makes of itself. From a structure-theoretical standpoint, the two oppositions are completely identical. With this, however, the value-opposition that is still associated today with the antithesis of dialectical idealism and dialectical materialism stands revealed as inauthentic.

The structural-theoretical identity of the two opposing positions is, of course, merely formal, and therefore does not seem to touch the irreconcilability of the value-opposition. This is a still widely held but mistaken view. The structural difference is far from a sufficient criterion for a genuine value-opposition — but in any case it is a necessary one. A formal structural difference alone would not suffice to constitute a genuine value-opposition; but its absence is fully sufficient to establish the absence of a genuine value-object.

Both worldviews — dialectical idealism as well as dialectical materialism — have grown out of the soil of German transcendental philosophy, whose frame is wide enough to encompass both possibilities and both interpretations of itself. In this respect both worldviews are hostile brothers, but their values are the same, even if they appear in opposite historical masks.

Now, it turns out that such a new level of interpretation of transcendental philosophy does not really even need to be discovered. It is not yet present as a fully developed theory, but, as I already hinted, it is already there in scientific practice — in the form of a novel conception of the relation between consciousness and world that has arisen on the ground of cybernetics.

Transcendental philosophy concerns itself — to put its concern in its simplest form — with the question: how can the transition from subject to object be understood cognitively? Cybernetics concerns itself with an exactly parallel question: how can properties such as memory, self-reflection, decision-making, perception of gestalt structures and so on — which up to now were taken as specific markers of an I-bearing system of subjectivity — be transferred onto physical machines, that is, onto mere objects? If problems of a transcendental logic are not involved here, then I must confess I do not know what transcendental philosophy is.

A side-remark may be in order at this point. A listener to my remarks may ask why I assign cybernetics such an extraordinary role — one that goes well beyond what one usually grants any single science, or even several, in terms of influence on a general worldview. The reason lies in the fact that under the collective name “cybernetics,” two fundamentally different things appear.

First: cybernetics can be regarded as a group of individual sciences — the most important being information theory, the theory of data-processing machines, communications engineering, and the study of long matrices. Second: hidden under the same term is a philosophical worldview that is simply applicable in every individual science, and that works with quite specific ontological viewpoints and logical methods. The most striking feature of cybernetics in this second sense is its interdisciplinary interest, and its tendency to dissolve the previous borders of the single sciences altogether. When I speak here of a cybernetic orientation of transcendental philosophy, I obviously mean cybernetics in this second and fundamental sense — a sense in which our entire universe is regarded as an enormous combinatorial mechanism that follows specific ontological and logical laws.

The logic of cybernetics departs from inherited thought-schemata insofar as it completely ignores classical pairs of concepts like spirit and matter, subject and object, transcendence and immanence, and in their place sets the simple distinction between system and environment. The cyberneticist observes that there exist in the world systems that possess an environment and that, via feedback mechanisms, are aware of themselves. Something logically novel arises in the interplay of system and environment; this interplay forms a kind of organizational center, whereby the organizational structure encompasses both the system and the environment. One may, if one wishes, designate this center as “I” or as “subjectivity.”

But if we ask where that center, which arises in the interplay of system and environment, is actually located, we arrive at the following interesting result: we may neither claim that its place is in the system, nor say that it is to be found in the environment. These two views would correspond most closely to the antithesis of idealism and materialism — if one still wants to apply this antiquated schema at all. It is more correct to say that the center is to be sought in the relation of system to environment. But even such a way of speaking remains imprecise. The relation between system and environment can attain a high degree of complexity. Since the theory of this relation is rather subtle, allow me a primitive example.

Let us compare the relation between system and environment to a band that holds the two together. Let this band also be marked off, like a tape measure. It then turns out that it is impossible to identify the border between objective environment and subjective system with any specific marking on the band. As conditions in system and environment change, the marked border will move closer to the system or closer to the environment. Theoretically it is possible for the border to slide all the way to the outermost ends of the band — so that the entire relational band must again be counted as belonging to the system, or to the environment.

If we count the marked band entirely as the system, then — as a rough approximation of older habits of thought — we can say that so-called subjectivity has its residence in a consciousness-system closed off from the environment. If, conversely, we count the marked band entirely as the environment, then with equal right we can say that subjectivity is wholly rooted in the objective environment. De facto, however, these are only theoretical limit cases to which, presumably, nothing in reality corresponds. The most adequate view is still to say that what we call “I” or subjectivity is comparable to a non-permanently-localizable mark on the relational band between system and environment.

But with this schema, a metaphysical presupposition common to idealism and materialism has been rejected. Both so-called worldviews assert — in quite astonishing unanimity — that the opposition of subject and object is logically to be reduced to one side of the opposition. Idealism asserts that the ultimate ground of the world is subjectivity, in which the objective appears only as a specific variant. Materialism asserts conversely that the ultimate ground of the world is its objectivity, in which subjectivity appears only as a specific property of objective appearance. The two thought-schemata are the same; relative to one another they are merely mirror-inverted.

The philosophical reflection that is now beginning to assert itself in cybernetics — and which need not at all be identified with cybernetics as a theory of machines — rejects the common problematic of idealism and materialism just described. But with this, more is rejected than a mere formal structure of two-valued thinking. In idealism just as in materialism, specific, mutually exclusive value-conceptions are implied. Their practical incompatibility is not abolished by the commonality of their formal structure; a philosophically oriented cyberneticist would maintain that the value-opposition of idealism and materialism is, on the basis of the cybernetic approach, completely irrelevant. In its place new valuations appear: for idealism the primal value is the realization of spirit; for materialism the primal value is the reliable objectivity of the material.

To relativize these values, and to reinterpret transcendental philosophy in this sense, is the task of the philosophy of the present. For the cyberneticist, neither pure spirituality nor primary materiality is the primal value, but rather the living, eternally shifting relation between system and environment; the respective location of the organizational center that holds system and environment together is for him the origin of all historical evaluation.

I do not believe that the philosophical work of an adequate adoption of transcendental philosophy can be accomplished in America or Russia in the foreseeable future. Here lies an enormous spiritual reservoir for German philosophy. Should it succeed in solving this task, then the philosophical thinking of the present — instead of, as is the case today, trotting along behind the positive sciences — would once again be in a position to take a leading role, and to furnish the individual sciences with new questions. And since such a philosophy could also anticipate future scientific developments, one could trust it to propose new organizational forms of scientific life — forms not merely tailored to the more or less accidental needs of our immediate present.

I would not, however, like to close this consideration without pointing out that the unique intellectual-historical situation in which German science finds itself at the present moment — namely, that transcendental philosophy was conceived precisely in Germany — can also have an eminent practical, indeed industrial significance. Lower conscious functions can today be represented in tolerable approximation by machines; but in the face of higher conscious functions, the ontological and logical theories existing up to now fail.

In this situation, two paths are open along which machine theory can be pushed forward. The slower and more expensive way is the experimental one: one tries all sorts of things until one finds what is right. It can be predicted with fair probability that, even with this cumbersome mode of working, in about ten years cybernetic machines with entirely new construction principles will appear on the market. That is to say, from around 1975 a wave of patents will likely come, concerning the construction of machines whose mode of operation reproduces — in astonishing approximation — even the higher conscious functions of the animal and human body.

The second possibility for scientific and technical progress in this field consists in the fundamental development of a transcendental theory that is applicable in machine technology. The seeds of such a theory have long been present in the German — and only in the German — tradition. All the problematics one needs have long since been pre-developed in the works of Kant, Fichte, Hegel and Schelling. It is only a matter of freeing the analyses present there from their time-bound formulations, and adopting them for practical use. What Germany contains in intellectual treasures is old, dusty equipment whose current practical value almost no one today suspects.

Here lies the possibility of international scientific cooperation. Abroad, people are seeking — without knowing it — a transcendental logic that is applicable to machines. The practical task of German philosophy would consist in reshaping inherited transcendental logic so that it becomes a useful export commodity for cybernetic needs. That would give Germany the opportunity to participate in the cybernetic patent wave, whose industrial value, even on a cautious estimate, would amount to more than 100 billion dollars a year. I am convinced that such a German cooperation would be welcomed abroad — again, for reasons of economic advantage. The experimental methods, sometimes extremely costly, could be substantially shortened. Here Germany has the chance to acquire fundamental patents from abroad.

In just under ten years, however, this chance will be irrevocably gone — the connection definitively missed. If German science does not seize this opportunity in the coming ten years, it will stagnate in a self-chosen provincialism, and Germany will sink industrially to a level at which it has to pay a heavily burdensome tribute abroad — in cybernetic licensing fees — every year. German philosophy, and with it German science, stands today at a crossroads. May God give it the strength to make the right decision.
